short: A brief, well-regarded reign remembered for disaster relief rather than the military reputation that preceded it.
full:
Titus succeeded his father Vespasian on 24 June 79 CE having already commanded the siege that crushed the Jewish revolt in 70 CE, a record that made senators wary of him as a potential tyrant. In office he governed mildly, reversing some of his father's harsher fiscal measures and personally organising relief after the eruption of Vesuvius that August and a further fire in Rome in 80 CE.

His reign lasted barely two years. Titus died of fever on 13 September 81 CE, the second consecutive Flavian succession to pass without contest, this time to his younger brother Domitian. Ancient writers, comparing him favourably to what followed, remembered him as the delight of the human race — a verdict later historians have treated with some caution given how short his rule was.
